title: The State of the Channel and Collection - 2020
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WjgW6u9Tde8

Year three. Daniel (@dungeondive) set out to average a video a week in 2019 and delivered nearly 80, which he counts as the year he found a rhythm. Growth was slower than hoped — he wanted 2,000 subscribers — and he diagnoses it plainly: this is a niche channel about one kind of game, broadening coverage would grow it faster, and he isn't interested in other kinds of games.

The most consequential passage is a policy decision on Kickstarter coverage. He will stop doing previews except for games he genuinely loves or badly wants funded, because the space is already saturated by channels doing exactly that, and he would rather talk about finished games than run advertisements.

The sell list is long and reasoned — Village Attacks on graphic design, Talisman 3rd edition on box size (the board is going on the wall as art), first-edition Warrior Knights because a five-hour competitive game will never hit his table. The additions include Cave Evil, bought openly as an art object he may never play, and Horrified, which he thinks he should have put in his top five: simple, strong, and a hit with non-gamers.

Running underneath is the constraint that shapes the channel — a very small house and a very tiny gaming room.

----

Is refusing to widen your subject matter for growth principled, or just an expensive preference?
